Evaluate at x = 11.00 ± 0.22 m, giving the two limits; the speed increases throughout this interval. Treat the ball and basket as points and neglect air resistance.

giancoli-ch3-q70.answer: Initial velocity ≈ 60.5 m/s at 60.8° above horizontal (about 61 m/s at 61°). Components are vx₀ = 195/6.6 = 29.5 m/s and vy₀ = [135 + ½(9.80)(6.6)²]/6.6 = 52.8 m/s.

giancoli-ch3-q72.answer: The rock hits the 45° downhill slope after t = 2vx/g = 2(15)/9.80 = 3.1 s. Set yrock = −½gt² equal to yslope = −x = −vxt and take the positive nonzero time.

giancoli-ch3-q74.answer: (a) vx₀ = 18 cos 42° = 13.4 m/s; vy₀ = 18 sin 42° = 12.0 m/s upward. (b) At the other building t = 55/vx₀ = 4.11 s, so the ball is ½gt² − vy₀t = 33 m below the rooftop. This assumes the wall extends down far enough for that intersection.

giancoli-ch4-q2.answer: Using W = mg: (a) Earth: 6.7 × 10² N; (b) Moon: 1.2 × 10² N; (c) Mars: 2.5 × 10² N. (d) Far from appreciable gravitational fields, weight is approximately zero. Constant velocity alone implies zero net force, not necessarily zero gravitational weight; location must be specified if gravity is significant.

giancoli-ch4-q4.answer: F = mΔv/Δt = (0.020)(0.35 − 0.25)/0.10 = 0.020 N. This is the simplified model's net accelerating force on the blood.

giancoli-ch4-q6.answer: The net force magnitude is ma = 65(30 × 9.80) = 1.9 × 10⁴ N, opposite the motion. The stopping distance at constant deceleration is v₀²/(2a) = (95/3.6)²/(2 × 30 × 9.80) = 1.2 m.

giancoli-ch4-q8.answer: Estimated average forward force ≈ 2.1 × 10² N. Starting from rest, a ≈ v²/(2d), so F ≈ mv²/(2d) = 7.0(13)²/(2 × 2.8) = 211 N. This estimates the forward component, neglecting height changes; the total hand force also supports the shot against gravity.

giancoli-ch4-q10.answer: The cable must withstand T = m(g + a) = 1200(9.80 + 0.70) = 1.26 × 10⁴ N.

giancoli-ch4-q12.answer: Acceleration is 1.84 m/s² upward: a = (T − mg)/m = 163/14.0 − 9.80. A downward-moving bucket with upward acceleration is slowing down.

giancoli-ch4-q14.answer: Maximum cable force = m(g + 0.0680g) = 5.08 × 10⁴ N; minimum = m(g − 0.0680g) = 4.43 × 10⁴ N. The extrema correspond to maximum upward and downward acceleration, respectively.

giancoli-ch4-q16.answer: Acceleration = 0.25g = 2.45 m/s² downward. Taking upward as positive, N − mg = ma and N = 0.75mg give a = −0.25g.

giancoli-ch4-q18.answer: Maximum upward acceleration = Tmax/m − g = 21750/2125 − 9.80 = 0.435 m/s².

giancoli-ch4-q20.answer: Table force: (a) 47.0 N upward; (b) 17.0 N upward; (c) 0 N. While the box remains on the table, N = 77.0 N − T and T equals the hanging weight. A 90.0-N hanging weight lifts the box, so the table loses contact rather than exerting a negative normal force.

giancoli-ch4-q22.answer: (a) During contact, draw gravity mg downward and the bat's contact force on the ball in its actual contact-force direction. (b) After contact, only mg acts downward when air resistance is ignored. There is no continuing force in the direction of flight supplied by the bat.

giancoli-ch4-q24.answer: (a) Pull downward with T = mg/2 = 353 N (about 350 N). Two rope segments provide upward tension to the combined person–bucket system. (b) A 15% larger pull gives 2(1.15T) − mg = ma, hence a = 0.15g = 1.47 m/s² upward. Assume an ideal pulley and rope.

giancoli-ch4-q26.answer: FB = 6.31 × 10³ N and |FA + FB| = 8.36 × 10³ N north. East–west balance gives FB sin 32° = 4500 sin 48°; the northward sum is 4500 cos 48° + FB cos 32°.

giancoli-ch4-q28.answer: (a) Fnet = (−10.2, −16.0) N, magnitude 19.0 N, 57.5° below −x; a = (−0.551, −0.865) m/s², magnitude 1.03 m/s². (b) F₁ is 30° below +x, so Fnet = (8.83, 10.9) N, magnitude 14.0 N at 51.0° above +x; a = (0.477, 0.589) m/s², magnitude 0.758 m/s².

giancoli-ch4-q30.answer: (a) A steady horizontal force of 9.9 N is needed. With sin θ = 0.15/4.0, equilibrium gives F = mg tan θ = 9.93 N. (b) T = mg/cos θ = 265 N. These are equilibrium values, assuming the chandelier is held at the displaced position.

giancoli-ch4-q32.answer: (a) Block A: mg down, normal force up, tension horizontally toward the pulley. Block B: mBg down and T up. (b) With A toward the pulley and B down positive, T = mAa and mBg − T = mBa. Therefore a = mBg/(mA + mB), and T = mAmBg/(mA + mB), for an ideal cord and pulley.

giancoli-ch4-q34.answer: (a) Each block has mg down and N up. Horizontally A has F forward and the contact from B backward; B has contact from A forward and from C backward; C has contact from B forward. (b) a = F/(mA + mB + mC). (c) Net forces are mAa, mBa, mCa forward. (d) The A–B contact magnitude is (mB + mC)a; the B–C contact magnitude is mCa; each pair acts in opposite directions. (e) a = 3.20 m/s²; each net force is 32.0 N; A–B contact is 64.0 N and B–C contact is 32.0 N. A pushes both trailing blocks, while B pushes only C.

giancoli-ch4-q38.answer: Minimum μs = a/g = 0.20. Static friction must supply ma, and its maximum is μsmg.

giancoli-ch4-q40.answer: Maximum deceleration magnitude = μsg = 0.75(9.80) = 7.35 m/s², about 7.4 m/s². Any larger value requires more static friction than is available.

giancoli-ch4-q42.answer: The box travels v₀²/(2μkg) = 3.5²/(2 × 0.15 × 9.80) = 4.2 m after the push ends, on a level floor.

giancoli-ch4-q44.answer: Estimated initial speed ≈ √(2μkgd) = √(2 × 0.80 × 9.80 × 72) = 34 m/s, or 121 km/h. Assume the wheels skid throughout and the final speed is approximately zero.

giancoli-ch4-q46.answer: Box A must have mass at least mB/μs = 2.0/0.30 = 6.7 kg. At rest the 2.0-kg hanging box requires T = mBg, and static friction on A can supply at most μsmAg.

giancoli-ch4-q48.answer: Mass ≈ 1.9 kg. At the threshold of downward slipping, upward friction is μsN and N = F cos 28°. Thus mg = F sin 28° + μsF cos 28°, giving m = 23(sin 28° + 0.40 cos 28°)/9.80 = 1.93 kg. The kinetic coefficient is not used at the static threshold.

giancoli-ch4-q50.answer: (a) Forces: weight downward, normal upward, applied force 45° below horizontal, friction backward. (b) Friction = 88.0 cos 45.0° = 62.2 N backward. (c) Normal force = mg + 88.0 sin 45.0° = 199 N. (d) For a = 1.5/2.5 = 0.60 m/s² and the stipulated unchanged friction, F = (ma + 62.2)/cos 45° = 99.9 N.

giancoli-ch4-q52.answer: (a) At rest: draw mg vertically down, N perpendicular outward from the plane, and static friction up the plane, balancing mg sin 33°. Its required value is mg sin 33°, not automatically μsN. (b) Sliding down: replace static friction with kinetic friction μkN up the plane. (c) Sliding up after release: kinetic friction points down the plane; there is no continuing shove force.

giancoli-ch4-q54.answer: Incline angle ≈ 12°. From s = v₀t + ½at², a = 2(18 − 2.0 × 3.3)/3.3² = 2.09 m/s². With negligible friction, sin θ = a/g, so θ = 12.3°.

giancoli-ch4-q56.answer: Friction = m(g sin 27° − a) = 104 N up the incline. The coefficient is μk = Ffr/(mg cos 27°) = 0.475, about 0.48.

giancoli-ch4-q58.answer: (a) Distance up the incline = v₀²/(2g sin 22.0°) = 2.8 m. (b) Total return time = 2v₀/(g sin 22.0°) = 2.5 s; ascent and descent times are equal because friction is absent.

giancoli-ch4-q60.answer: (a) Uphill distance = v₀²/[2g(sin 25.0° + 0.12 cos 25.0°)] = 0.86 m. (b) Total return time ≈ 1.3 s: uphill deceleration is 5.21 m/s² and downhill acceleration is 3.08 m/s², so t = 3.0/5.21 + √(2 × 0.864/3.08) = 1.33 s. Assume the crate begins sliding back at the turning point; static friction is not specified.

giancoli-ch4-q62.answer: μk = tan 12° = 0.213, about 0.21. Constant speed means mg sin 12° = μkmg cos 12°, with negligible air resistance.

giancoli-ch4-q64.answer: Only the 6.0° driveway is safe in the ideal static-friction model. No slipping requires tan θ ≤ μs = 0.15, or θ ≤ arctan(0.15) = 8.53°. Both 9.0° and 12° exceed this limit.

giancoli-ch4-q66.answer: μk = ¾ tan 34° = 0.506, about 0.51. Starting from rest over the same distance, v²/vfrictionless² = (sin θ − μk cos θ)/sin θ = 1/4, which gives the result.

giancoli-ch4-q68.answer: The average upward air-resistance force over the fall distance is 6.3 N: Favg = mg − mv²/(2h) = 2.0(9.80) − 2.0(27)²/(2 × 55) = 6.35 N. This is a distance average, or the equivalent constant resisting force; the time average cannot be found from the supplied data without a drag model.

giancoli-ch4-q70.answer: (a), (b), and (c): 735 N, displayed as 75.0 kg, because acceleration is zero. (d) Accelerating up at 3.0 m/s²: 960 N, displayed as 98.0 kg. (e) Accelerating down at 3.0 m/s²: 510 N, displayed as 52.0 kg. Use N = m(g + ay), and a scale's kg reading is N/g.

giancoli-ch4-q72.answer: An uphill driving force of about 1.4 × 10² N is needed. Steady downhill motion implies air drag = mg sin 6.5°; uphill at the same speed, gravity and the same drag both oppose motion. Thus F = 2mg sin 6.5° = 144 N.

giancoli-ch4-q74.answer: (a) The midpoint sag must be at least 1.53 m. From 2T sin θ = mg and tan θ = x/12.5, use the recommended limit T = 2.9 kN. (b) At one-quarter of that sag, x = 0.383 m, T = mg√(12.5² + x²)/(2x) = 11.5 kN. It exceeds the recommended 2.9 kN but is below the stated 29 kN breaking tension, so it does not break in this ideal static calculation.

giancoli-ch4-q76.answer: (a) The limiting lifting force is F = Mg/2; a force infinitesimally above this starts upward acceleration. (b) At the threshold, FT₁ = FT₂ = Mg/2, FT₄ = Mg, and FT₃ = 3Mg/2. The two equal-tension strands support the lower pulley; the upper support carries both strands around the upper pulley plus the anchored strand attached to its hook.

giancoli-ch4-q78.answer: Seat force ≈ 867 N, directed 18.2° forward from vertical. With horizontal x and vertical y, Fseat = (ma cos 18°, m[g + a sin 18°]) = (271, 823) N. Its magnitude is √(271² + 823²); assume no other contact force acts on the pilot.

giancoli-ch4-q80.answer: Cable tension = m[g + v₀²/(2d)] = 1450[9.80 + 3.5²/(2 × 2.6)] = 1.76 × 10⁴ N, approximately 1.8 × 10⁴ N. The downward-moving elevator accelerates upward as it stops.

giancoli-ch4-q82.answer: Required time = mΔv/F = (1.0 × 10¹⁰)(0.0020)/2.5 = 8.0 × 10⁶ s, about 93 days. The tug must act in a direction that supplies the required velocity change.

giancoli-ch4-q84.answer: The upward acceleration must satisfy 0.771 < a ≤ 1.029 m/s². The 2.10-kg line breaks only when 2.10(g + a) > 22.2 N; the 2.05-kg line survives when 2.05(g + a) ≤ 22.2 N. The other masses then behave as described automatically.

giancoli-ch4-q86.answer: μs ≈ 0.36. The threshold deceleration is (45/3.6)/3.5 = 3.57 m/s², and μs = a/g = 0.364.

giancoli-ch4-q88.answer: Yes. The stopping distance is v₀²/(2μkg) = 29.2 m, greater than 15 m. The exit speed is √[20.0² − 2(0.70)(9.80)(15)] = 13.9 m/s, about 14 m/s, under the stated sliding-friction model.

giancoli-ch4-q90.answer: (a) Sand mass = μsmblock − mbucket = 0.45(28.0) − 2.00 = 10.6 kg. (b) Once sliding starts, a = g(mhanging − μkmblock)/(mblock + mhanging) = 0.879 m/s², bucket downward. Use the full hanging mass 12.6 kg, including the bucket.

giancoli-ch4-q92.answer: Incline acceleration = g(sin 28° − 0.18 cos 28°) = 3.04 m/s² downhill. The speed at the bottom is √[5.0² + 2(3.0433)(110)] = 26.4 m/s. On the flat the acceleration is −0.15g = −1.47 m/s² along the motion, giving x = v²/(2 × 1.47) = 236 m, about 2.4 × 10² m.

giancoli-ch4-q94.answer: (a) Common downhill acceleration = g[sin 32° − (0.20 + 0.30)cos 32°/2] = 3.12 m/s². (b) Cord tension = mAg sin 32° − μAmAg cos 32° − mAa = 2.08 N. The cord pulls the lower, less-frictional block A uphill and the upper block B downhill.

giancoli-ch4-q96.answer: Initial speed = √(2μkgd) = √[2(0.10)(9.80)(75)] = 12 m/s, on level ice with the stated constant coefficient.

giancoli-ch5-q2.answer: a = v²/r = 525²/5200 = 53.0 m/s², or 5.41g, directed toward the center of the pullout arc.

giancoli-ch5-q4.answer: a = ω²r = (2π × 45/60)²(0.175) = 3.9 m/s² toward the wheel's axis.

giancoli-ch5-q6.answer: Required rotation rate = (60/2π)√(125000g/0.0700) = 3.99 × 10⁴ rpm, approximately 40,000 rpm.

giancoli-ch5-q8.answer: Minimum μs = v²/(rg) = (95/3.6)²/(125 × 9.80) = 0.57. Static friction supplies the centripetal force.

giancoli-ch5-q10.answer: (a) At the bottom, T − mg = mv²/r, giving v = √[(25.0 − 19.6)(1.20)/2.00] = 1.80 m/s. (b) At the top, the limiting speed for a taut rope is √(gr) = 3.43 m/s; a slightly greater speed gives positive tension. The given bottom speed is insufficient to complete a freely swinging full circle.

giancoli-ch5-q12.answer: (a) Minimum radius = v²/(6g) = (840/3.6)²/(6 × 9.80) ≈ 9.3 × 10² m. (b) At the bottom, seat force = m(g + 6g) = 5.4 × 10³ N upward. (c) At the top, seat force toward the center = m(6g − g) = 3.8 × 10³ N downward, assuming the same speed and this limiting radius.

giancoli-ch5-q14.answer: Each skater pulls with F = m(2π/T)²r = 55.0(2π/2.5)²(0.80) ≈ 2.8 × 10² N. Each circles the midpoint, at radius 0.80 m; the pair of hand forces have equal magnitude, not twice this value.

giancoli-ch5-q16.answer: For a constant-speed circular transition all the way to the 18° downhill slope, r ≥ v²/(g cos 18°) = 75 m. The normal force is N = m[g cos φ − v²/r], whose minimum occurs at the steepest part. If only the horizontal crest is considered, the limiting estimate is v²/g = 71 m; maintaining contact over the entire stated transition requires the larger value.

giancoli-ch5-q18.answer: Maximum bottom speed = √[(Fmax/m − g)L] = √[(1150/78 − 9.80)(4.7)] = 4.8 m/s. At the bottom the vine must support weight as well as supply centripetal force.

giancoli-ch5-q20.answer: Estimated radius ≈ 28 m. Table 4–2 gives μs ≈ 0.7 for rubber on wet concrete; r = v²/(μsg) = (50/3.6)²/(0.7 × 9.80). This uses the limiting static-friction speed and no additional safety margin.

giancoli-ch5-q22.answer: Minimum μs ≈ 0.315, or 0.32. The bank angle obeys tan θ = (65/3.6)²/(95g) = 0.350. At 95 km/h friction acts down the bank; μs = [v²/(rg) − tan θ]/[1 + (v²/(rg))tan θ].

giancoli-ch5-q24.answer: Tangential force = mΔv/Δt = 950(35/11) = 3.0 × 10³ N along the motion. Radial force = mv²/r = 950(15²/500) = 4.3 × 10² N inward. Example 5–8 supplies the 35 m/s in 11 s acceleration and 500 m track radius; vertical forces balance.

giancoli-ch5-q26.answer: (a) Draw radial acceleration inward and tangential acceleration forward along the path; their vector sum points inward and forward. (b) At constant speed, tangential acceleration is zero and total acceleration equals the inward radial acceleration. (c) Draw radial acceleration inward and tangential acceleration backward; the total points inward and backward. In every case aR = v²/r and atan = dv/dt.

giancoli-ch5-q28.answer: Gravity force ≈ 2.02 × 10³ N toward Earth's center. At an altitude of 2RE the center-to-center distance is 3RE, so F = mg/9, not mg/4.

giancoli-ch5-q30.answer: The zero-force point lies about 3.46 × 10⁸ m from Earth's center, or 3.83 × 10⁷ m from the Moon's center along the line between them. Solve ME/x² = MM/(D − x)², giving x = D/[1 + √(MM/ME)], with D ≈ 3.84 × 10⁸ m. If measured from Earth's surface, subtract RE to get about 3.39 × 10⁸ m.

giancoli-ch5-q32.answer: Surface gravity is gEarth/4 = 2.45 m/s², approximately 2.5 m/s², because g = GM/R² and the radius doubles while mass remains unchanged.

giancoli-ch5-q34.answer: Estimated Europa surface gravity ≈ 2.0 m/s². Equal mean density gives REuropa/REarth = (MEuropa/MEarth)^(1/3), so gEuropa/gEarth = (4.9 × 10²²/5.98 × 10²⁴)^(1/3). This is the estimate under the stipulated Earth-density assumption.

giancoli-ch5-q36.answer: Net gravitational force on the Moon ≈ 4.77 × 10²⁰ N, directed 24.6° from the Moon–Sun direction toward Earth. The perpendicular components are FME ≈ 1.99 × 10²⁰ N and FMS ≈ 4.34 × 10²⁰ N, using distances 3.84 × 10⁸ m and 1.50 × 10¹¹ m; combine by Pythagoras and tan θ = FME/FMS.

giancoli-ch5-q38.answer: Surface g becomes 2/9 of its original value: gnew/gold = (2M/M)/(3R/R)² = 2/9.

giancoli-ch5-q40.answer: Gravity at 380 km altitude is about 0.891 of surface gravity, only 10.9% weaker. Use g(h)/g(0) = [RE/(RE + h)]² with RE ≈ 6380 km. Orbiting astronauts feel weightless because they and the shuttle are in continuous free fall, not because gravity vanishes.

giancoli-ch5-q42.answer: Net force ≈ 1.1 × 10⁻⁸ N toward the square's center, along the diagonal. Each adjacent sphere contributes F₀ = Gm²/a²; the opposite sphere adds F₀/2 along the same diagonal, giving F = (√2 + 1/2)F₀.

giancoli-ch5-q44.answer: Surface gravity ≈ 6.6 × 10¹² m/s² using g = G(5MSun)/(10⁴ m)². This is roughly 7 × 10¹¹ times Earth's surface gravity in the Newtonian estimate requested.

giancoli-ch5-q46.answer: Circular-orbit speed ≈ 5.97 × 10³ m/s, about 6.0 km/s. Use v = √[GME/(RE + 4800 km)] with center-to-center orbital radius ≈ 1.118 × 10⁷ m.

giancoli-ch5-q48.answer: The limiting upward acceleration is 185/12.0 − 9.80 = 5.62 m/s². The cord breaks when the upward acceleration exceeds this value, since T = m(g + a). Downward acceleration reduces tension.

giancoli-ch5-q50.answer: The satellite at 7500 km altitude is faster by a factor √[(RE + 15000 km)/(RE + 7500 km)] ≈ 1.24. Use distance from Earth's center, not altitude alone, in v = √(GME/r).

giancoli-ch5-q52.answer: Period ≈ 2π√(RE/g) = 5.07 × 10³ s, or 84.5 min, approximately 85 min. The satellite's mass cancels and does not affect this ideal circular-orbit period.

giancoli-ch5-q54.answer: (a) At the top, apparent/real weight = 1 − 4π²r/(gT²) = 0.716. (b) At the bottom it is 1 + 4π²r/(gT²) = 1.284. Use r = 11.0 m and T = 12.5 s.

giancoli-ch5-q56.answer: (a) Circular motion requires 4π²R/T² = GM/R². Substituting M = 4πR³ρ/3 and canceling R yields ρ = 3π/(GT²). (b) With T = 85 min, ρ ≈ 5.43 × 10³ kg/m³, about 5.4 g/cm³.

giancoli-ch5-q58.answer: Mean orbital distance, meaning semimajor axis, ≈ 1.08 AU = 1.62 × 10¹¹ m. Kepler's law relative to Earth gives a/AU = (410/365.25)^(2/3).

giancoli-ch5-q60.answer: Earth's mass ≈ 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg from ME ≈ 4π²rMoon³/(GTMoon²), using rMoon ≈ 3.84 × 10⁸ m and TMoon ≈ 27.3 days. This approximation neglects the Moon's mass; a two-body calculation gives ME + MM before MM is subtracted.

giancoli-ch5-q62.answer: (a) Io gives MJ = 1.902 × 10²⁷ kg. (b) Europa gives 1.901 × 10²⁷ kg, Ganymede 1.895 × 10²⁷ kg, and Callisto 1.898 × 10²⁷ kg. All agree to about 0.4%, consistent with the rounded data. For each use MJ ≈ 4π²r³/(GT²), with distances in meters and periods in seconds.

giancoli-ch5-q64.answer: vA/vB = √(rB/rA) = 1/√7.0 ≈ 0.38, since circular orbital speed varies as r^(−1/2).

giancoli-ch5-q66.answer: (a) Semimajor axis a = 2400^(2/3) AU ≈ 179 AU. (b) Farthest distance = 2a − rnear ≈ 358 AU. (c) Conservation of angular momentum at the apsides gives vnear/vfar = rfar/rnear ≈ 358. The closest distance is approximately 1.0 AU, so these estimates have only a few significant figures.

giancoli-ch5-q68.answer: If the hanging mass is stationary, the cord tension is T = mg. For the puck the same tension supplies centripetal force: T = Mv²/R. Equating them gives v = √(mgR/M), assuming an ideal cord, hole, and frictionless table.

giancoli-ch5-q70.answer: Yes. A friction force of about 5.40 × 10³ N must act down the bank, toward the curve's center and downward. Resolving forces gives Ffr = m[(v²/r)cos 14° − g sin 14°], with v = 85/3.6 m/s. The frictionless design speed would be only 47.8 km/h.

giancoli-ch5-q72.answer: The line makes an angle of 56° with vertical. For a conical pendulum, Tline cos θ = mg and Tline sin θ = mω²L sin θ, giving cos θ = g/(ω²L) = g(0.75)²/(4π² × 0.25).

giancoli-ch5-q74.answer: (a) On the unbanked train, required friction is mv²/r = 191 N inward. (b) With the floor tilted 8.0° toward the center, required friction is m[(v²/r)cos 8° − g sin 8°] = 114 N down the tilted floor toward the center. Use 160 km/h = 44.4 m/s.

giancoli-ch5-q76.answer: Altitude h = (√2 − 1)RE ≈ 2.64 × 10⁶ m, or 2640 km. Set [RE/(RE + h)]² = 1/2.

giancoli-ch5-q78.answer: A day would last about 85 min (1.4 h). Apparent equatorial weight is zero when ω²RE = g, hence T = 2π√(RE/g). This ignores Earth's deformation and any change in its gravitational field.

giancoli-ch5-q80.answer: Orbital period ≈ 118 min, about 2.0 h. Use T = 2π√[r³/(GMMoon)] with r = 1.74 × 10⁶ + 1.00 × 10⁵ m and MMoon = 7.35 × 10²² kg.

giancoli-ch5-q82.answer: Using the stated dimensions as a rectangular-volume estimate: (a) equivalent spherical radius ≈ 7.0 km; (b) surface g ≈ 4.5 × 10⁻³ m/s²; (c) orbital period at center-to-center radius 20 km ≈ 10.5 h.
steps: V ≈ (40 × 6 × 6) km³ = 1.44 × 10¹² m³; M = ρV = 3.31 × 10¹⁵ kg. Then R = (3V/4π)^(1/3), g = GM/R², and Torbit = 2π√(rorbit³/GM).
assumptions: The irregular asteroid is approximated by a box for its volume. An ellipsoid using the same full dimensions instead gives R ≈ 5.65 km, g ≈ 3.63 × 10⁻³ m/s², and period ≈ 14.5 h; the question requests an estimate.

giancoli-ch5-q84.answer: Estimated enclosed galactic mass ≈ 3.4 × 10⁴¹ kg, corresponding to about 1.7 × 10¹¹ solar-mass stars. Use M = 4π²r³/(GT²), r = 30000(9.5 × 10¹⁵) m and T = 2.0 × 10⁸ years. This is the enclosed-mass estimate under the stated central-mass model; real galaxies also contain dark matter.

giancoli-ch5-q86.answer: Core mass ≈ 5.2 × 10³⁹ kg, or 2.6 × 10⁹ solar masses. A circular gas orbit gives M = v²r/G with v = 7.80 × 10⁵ m/s and r = 5.7 × 10¹⁷ m.

giancoli-ch5-q88.answer: The ring's rotation period is about 9.0 Earth days. The floor must exert an inward normal force mg while solar gravity also acts inward, so ω²r = g + GMSun/r². With r ≈ 1.50 × 10¹¹ m, T = 2π√[r/(g + GMSun/r²)] ≈ 7.77 × 10⁵ s. Neglecting the much smaller solar gravity gives essentially the same estimate.

giancoli-ch5-q90.answer: Let aR = C vᵖrᑫ. Comparing dimensions gives LT⁻² = L^(p+q)T⁻ᵖ, so p = 2 and q = −1. Thus aR = C v²/r. Dimensional analysis determines the form but cannot determine the dimensionless constant; circular-motion geometry gives C = 1.

giancoli-ch6-q2.answer: Maximum work on the nail = mgh = 1.2(9.80)(0.50) = 5.9 J, if all the falling head's mechanical energy reaches the nail. Applying a downward force supplies additional work and increases the impact energy beyond mgh.

giancoli-ch6-q4.answer: (a) Work = Ffrd = 230(5.0) = 1.15 × 10³ J. (b) Work = Wh = 1200(5.0) = 6.0 × 10³ J. Constant speed makes net work zero; these are the required external positive works.

giancoli-ch6-q6.answer: Estimated work ≈ 6.0 × 10³ J. The cutting distance is lawn area / mower width = (10 × 20)/0.50 = 400 m; W ≈ Fd = 15(400). Ignore overlap, turns, and any vertical force component.

giancoli-ch6-q8.answer: For a small rotation Δθ, input and output distances are lIΔθ and lOΔθ. Equal ideal input and output work gives FI lIΔθ = FO lOΔθ, hence FO/FI = lI/lO. The forces must act perpendicular to the corresponding lever motion, or use their effective perpendicular components.

giancoli-ch6-q10.answer: (a) Man's force = mg sin 25° = 1.6 × 10³ N uphill. (b) His work = −mg(2.9)sin 25° = −4.6 × 10³ J. (c) Gravity does +4.6 × 10³ J. (d) Net work is zero, consistent with constant speed; the normal force does no work.

giancoli-ch6-q12.answer: Gravity does Wg = −mgL sin 12° = −245 J; the normal force does zero work; the push does +245 J. The push is 29° from the uphill displacement, so FP cos 29° = mg sin 12°, and WP = FP L cos 29°. Assume no rolling resistance as none is specified.

giancoli-ch6-q14.answer: (a) Engine work = (130 kN)(85 m) = 1.11 × 10⁷ J. (b) Catapult work is the trapezoid area under its force–distance graph: ½(1100 + 65) kN × 85 m = 4.95 × 10⁷ J.

giancoli-ch6-q16.answer: (a) Speed increases by √3 ≈ 1.73, since K ∝ v² for fixed mass. (b) Halving speed makes kinetic energy one-quarter of its initial value.

giancoli-ch6-q18.answer: Net stopping work = −½mv² = −½(925)(95/3.6)² = −3.22 × 10⁵ J. The brakes and other resisting forces must remove about 3.2 × 10⁵ J of kinetic energy.

giancoli-ch6-q20.answer: Average force on the glove ≈ 3.0 × 10² N in the incoming ball's direction. Favgd = ½mv² gives Favg = 0.145(32)²/(2 × 0.25) = 297 N. The glove exerts the equal, opposite stopping force on the ball.

giancoli-ch6-q22.answer: Braking distance becomes 1.50² = 2.25 times its original value, an increase of 125%, if the same braking deceleration applies and reaction time is excluded.

giancoli-ch6-q24.answer: The heavier car initially travels at 5.7 m/s and the lighter at 11 m/s. Let their masses be 2m and m: half the kinetic energy implies vlight = 2vheavy. Equality after both gain 8.0 m/s gives 2(vheavy + 8)² = (2vheavy + 8)², so vheavy = 8/√2 = 5.66 m/s.

giancoli-ch6-q26.answer: Gravitational potential energy increases by ΔU = mgΔh = 54(9.80)(4.0) = 2.1 × 10³ J.

giancoli-ch6-q28.answer: Additional work = 48 J. Spring energy scales as x²; stretching from 0 to 6.0 cm requires 6.0(6.0/2.0)² = 54 J in total, so the added work beyond 2.0 cm is 54 − 6 = 48 J.

giancoli-ch6-q30.answer: (a) Uground = mg(2.20) = 35.6 J. (b) Uhead = mg(2.20 − 1.60) = 9.70 J. (c) For lifting from rest to rest without losses, the person does 35.6 J, equal to ΔU for either reference. With head-level zero, the initial potential is −25.9 J, so the change remains 35.6 J.

giancoli-ch6-q32.answer: Jane can rise h = v²/(2g) = 5.0²/(2 × 9.80) = 1.3 m above her grab point, provided the vine stays taut and lets her reach a turning point. The energy-limited rise does not depend on length. An exceptionally short vine can lose tension or constrain the trajectory, so the ordinary swing assumption matters.

giancoli-ch6-q34.answer: Minimum takeoff speed = √(vtop² + 2gΔh) = √(0.50² + 2 × 9.80 × 2.10) = 6.44 m/s, neglecting losses.

giancoli-ch6-q36.answer: (a) At the top only horizontal speed remains: vtop = 8.8 cos 36° = 7.1 m/s. (b) From energy, mgh = ½m(v₀² − vtop²), so h = 1.4 m above the release point. Neglect air resistance.

giancoli-ch6-q38.answer: (a) Speed on first contacting the trampoline = √(4.5² + 2g × 2.0) = 7.7 m/s downward. (b) Maximum depression x = 0.26 m: solve ½kx² = ½mvimpact² + mgx with m = 62 kg and k = 5.8 × 10⁴ N/m. Gravity continues doing work during compression.

giancoli-ch6-q40.answer: Speeds: at point 2, 25 m/s; at point 3, 11 m/s; at point 4, 19 m/s. From the diagram the heights are 32, 0, 26, and 14 m, and energy gives vi = √[2g(32 − hi)] after release from rest.

giancoli-ch6-q42.answer: Spring constant k = m amax²/v₀² = 2.65 × 10³ N/m, approximately 2.6 × 10³ N/m. Use ½mv₀² = ½kxmax² and kxmax/m = 4.0g. This ideal design needs a very large compression xmax = v₀²/(4g) ≈ 17.8 m; other resisting forces are neglected.

giancoli-ch6-q44.answer: (a) Maximum speed is √[v₀² + (k/m)x₀²], attained at equilibrium. (b) Maximum displacement magnitude is A = √[x₀² + (m/k)v₀²]. Both follow from ½mv² + ½kx² = ½mv₀² + ½kx₀²; extension reaches +A and compression reaches −A in ideal oscillation.

giancoli-ch6-q46.answer: Mechanical energy converted to internal energy = 2(½mv²) = 3.68 × 10⁷ J, about 3.7 × 10⁷ J, using m = 66000 kg for each car and v = 85/3.6 m/s. In practice it becomes heat, deformation, and sound rather than exclusively immediate thermal energy.

giancoli-ch6-q48.answer: (a) Bottom speed = √[2gL(sin 28° − 0.090 cos 28°)] = 25.5 m/s. (b) Level stopping distance = v²/(2μkg) = 368 m, about 3.7 × 10² m. Gravity's downhill work minus friction gives the initial kinetic energy for the level section.

giancoli-ch6-q50.answer: Speed at point 2 = √[1.30² + 2g(32 − 0.23 × 45.0)] = 20.6 m/s. The gravitational height drop is 32 m, while friction does work −0.23mg(45.0 m) along the track.

giancoli-ch6-q52.answer: (a) Fraction lost = 1 − 1.6/2.0 = 0.20, or 20%. (b) Speed just before impact = √(2g × 2.0) = 6.3 m/s downward; just after = √(2g × 1.6) = 5.6 m/s upward. (c) The lost mechanical energy becomes internal energy in the ball and floor, deformation, and sound. Ignore air resistance.

giancoli-ch6-q54.answer: Impact speed = √(165² + 2 × 9.80 × 135) = 173 m/s. In the absence of air resistance, only the height change and initial speed enter energy conservation; the launch angle does not affect impact speed.

giancoli-ch6-q56.answer: (a) Without air resistance, landing speed = √[(480/3.6)² + 2g(3500)] = 294 m/s, or 1060 km/h. (b) Energy lost divided by glide-path length gives average drag ≈ 2.42 × 10³ N. Use path length 3500/sin 12° and energy loss ½m(vi² − vf²) + mgh, with vf = 210/3.6 m/s. This is an ideal constant-angle path estimate.

giancoli-ch6-q58.answer: (a) 1 hp = 550 ft·lbf/s = 550(0.3048 m)(4.44822 N)/s = 745.7 W ≈ 746 W. (b) A 75-W bulb is rated at 75/746 = 0.101 hp of electrical input power; this is not its visible-light output alone.

giancoli-ch6-q60.answer: Average resisting force = P/v = 18(746)/(95/3.6) = 509 N, about 5.1 × 10² N, opposite the motion. At steady speed the driving force balances it.

giancoli-ch6-q62.answer: Average power into the shot's kinetic energy = ΔK/Δt = ½(7.3)(14)²/1.5 = 477 W, about 4.8 × 10² W. Any elevation work would require extra information.

giancoli-ch6-q64.answer: Work = Pt = 2.0(746)(3600) = 5.4 × 10⁶ J in one hour, assuming the 2.0 hp is mechanical output.

giancoli-ch6-q66.answer: Average power ≈ mgh/t = 82(9.80)(83 sin 33°)/75 = 4.8 × 10² W. This is mechanical power against gravity; metabolic power is greater.

giancoli-ch6-q68.answer: Approximately 1.9 MW of useful lifting power, assuming an average passenger mass of 75 kg. P = (47000/3600 people/s)(75 kg)(9.80)(200 m).
assumptions: The figure is an estimate for lifting passengers only. Lift equipment, friction, and motor inefficiency increase the actual installed power; the question gives no passenger mass or efficiencies.

giancoli-ch6-q70.answer: Minimum mechanical power = μkmgv = 0.45(370)(9.80)(1.20) = 1.96 kW = 2.62 hp, about 2.6 hp. This assumes no additional losses.

giancoli-ch6-q72.answer: Effective spring constant ≈ mv²/x² = 10⁴(60/3.6)²/(500)² = 11 N/m. Equate the train's initial kinetic energy with the elastic energy ½kx²; this is the combined effective web stiffness.

giancoli-ch6-q74.answer: Maximum rise above release ≈ W/(mg) = 80.0/(1.85 × 9.80) = 4.41 m if the stated 80.0 J becomes the rock's kinetic energy at release. If 80.0 J instead includes raising the rock during the hand's throwing motion, subtract that pre-release gain in gravitational energy before using this formula; its distance is not specified.

giancoli-ch6-q76.answer: (a) Gravity does mgh = 2.58 × 10⁵ J before contact. (b) Impact speed = √(2gh) = 23.6 m/s. (c) Maximum spring compression = 2.66 m, from ½kx² = mg(28.5 + x). Assume the elevator starts from rest when the cable breaks and neglect losses.

giancoli-ch6-q78.answer: Estimated external mechanical power = mgv sin 12° = 75(9.80)(3.1/3.6)sin 12° ≈ 132 W, comparable to a 130-W lightbulb. The patient's metabolic power is higher because muscular efficiency is below 100%.

giancoli-ch6-q80.answer: Required effective bumper stiffness = mv²/xmax² = 1050(8/3.6)²/(0.015)² = 2.3 × 10⁷ N/m. Equate ½mv² to ½kxmax² for the stated elastic wall-impact test.

giancoli-ch6-q82.answer: Time = 7.6 s. At constant power, time is proportional to Δ(v²), so t₂ = 3.8(95² − 55²)/(65² − 35²) = 7.6 s; using the same speed units in the ratio is sufficient.

giancoli-ch6-q84.answer: Minimum launch speed = √(6.5² + 2g × 1.1) = 8.0 m/s. At the top of the flight the vertical component is zero, and the remaining kinetic energy corresponds to the stated 6.5 m/s.

giancoli-ch6-q86.answer: (a) Horizontal launch speed at B = √[2g(45.0 − 4.4)] = 28.2 m/s. (b) Landing distance along the 30° slope is s ≈ 116 m. Relative to B, write x = vt and y = −½gt²; the slope is y = −4.4 − x tan 30°. Solving their intersection gives x ≈ 101 m, then s = x/cos 30°. Neglect friction and drag.

giancoli-ch6-q88.answer: Ideal peak scale reading ≈ 4.5 × 10⁴ N, about 59 times the person's ordinary weight. The spring constant is k = 760/0.00060 N/m. If the person lands from rest after falling 1.0 m to the initially uncompressed scale, ½kx² = 760(1.0 + x); the peak reading kx is 4.46 × 10⁴ N. A real scale and human body are not ideal springs at this loading.

giancoli-ch6-q90.answer: (a) Bottom speed = √(2gl). (b) With h = 0.80l, the new circular radius is l − h = 0.20l, and its top is 0.60l below the original release point. Thus vtop = √[2g(2h − l)] = √(1.20gl). Tension is positive there, so the taut-circle assumption is consistent.

giancoli-ch6-q92.answer: (a) Release angle from vertical: θ = arccos[1 − v₀²/(2gL)] = 35.3°. (b) Tension just before release = mg cos θ = 448 N, since the speed is zero there. (c) Maximum tension occurs at the bottom: T = mg + mv₀²/L = 750 N. Use m = 56 kg, L = 10.0 m, v₀ = 6.0 m/s.

giancoli-ch6-q94.answer: Average drag ≈ 1.8 N opposite the pitch. The work-energy relation gives Favg = m(vi² − vf²)/(2d) = 0.25[(120/3.6)² − (0.90 × 120/3.6)²]/(2 × 15) = 1.76 N. This is the average over distance, with gravity neglected as stipulated.

giancoli-ch7-q2.answer: Change in velocity = −Ft/m = −25(15)/65 = −5.8 m/s along the initial motion. This assumes the skier remains moving throughout the 15 s; friction cannot reverse a skier who has already stopped.

giancoli-ch7-q4.answer: Mutual speed = 0.70 m/s in the halfback's original direction. Taking the tackler's direction positive, vf = [110(2.5) − 82(5.0)]/(110 + 82) = −0.703 m/s.

giancoli-ch7-q6.answer: Second car's mass = m₁(v₁/vf − 1) = 7700(14/5.0 − 1) = 1.4 × 10⁴ kg, from momentum conservation for a sticking collision.

giancoli-ch7-q8.answer: Recoiling nucleus speed = vα/57 = 4.9 × 10³ m/s, opposite to the alpha particle. Their momenta must be equal and opposite because the original nucleus was at rest.

giancoli-ch7-q10.answer: The fragment with twice the kinetic energy has half the mass: mhigh-energy/mlow-energy = 1/2. Their momentum magnitudes are equal, and K = p²/(2m).

giancoli-ch7-q12.answer: Average bat force on the ball is about 2.13 × 10³ N, directed 42.7° upward from the direction opposite the incoming pitch. Taking the incoming velocity as +x, its components are Fx = −1.57 × 10³ N and Fy ≈ +1.44 × 10³ N. The outgoing vertical speed is √(2g × 31.5) = 24.8 m/s; use Fbat = mΔv/Δt − mg-vector, with Δt = 0.0025 s. Gravity contributes only about 1.4 N during contact.

giancoli-ch7-q14.answer: (a) The sections travel at 5.20 × 10³ m/s and 8.00 × 10³ m/s, both away from Earth. Equal masses have speeds 1400 m/s below and above the original 6600 m/s. (b) Added kinetic energy = M(vrelative)²/8 = 725(2800)²/8 = 7.11 × 10⁸ J; neglect external impulse during the explosion.

giancoli-ch7-q16.answer: (a) Impulse = mΔv = 0.045(38) = 1.7 N·s along the shot. (b) Average force = impulse/Δt = 1.71/(3.5 × 10⁻³) = 4.9 × 10² N.

giancoli-ch7-q18.answer: Impulse magnitude = 2mv cos 45° = 2.4 N·s, perpendicular to and away from the wall. The velocity component parallel to the wall is unchanged; the normal component reverses.

giancoli-ch7-q20.answer: Additional impact force ≈ (dm/dt)v = [1000(1.0)(0.025)/3600](8.0) = 0.056 N downward on the pan. The weight of water already accumulated is a separate contribution, not part of the impact force.

giancoli-ch7-q22.answer: Required impulse from rest = mΔv = 0.50(3.0) = 1.5 N·s, in the throwing direction.

giancoli-ch7-q24.answer: (a) Net stopping impulse = m√(2gh) = 4.1 × 10² N·s upward. (b) For a 1.0-cm stopping distance, average ground force = mg(1 + h/d) = 1.51 × 10⁵ N upward. (c) For a 0.50-m stopping distance it is 3.56 × 10³ N upward. These forces follow from stopping work and are distance averages, or constant-force estimates; exact time-averaged forces require the impact force history.

giancoli-ch7-q26.answer: The 0.450-kg puck rebounds west at 1.93 m/s; the 0.900-kg puck moves east at 3.87 m/s. Use v₁′ = (m₁ − m₂)v₁/(m₁ + m₂) and v₂′ = 2m₁v₁/(m₁ + m₂) for the elastic collision.

giancoli-ch7-q28.answer: The balls exchange velocities. The ball initially moving +2.00 m/s leaves at −3.60 m/s, and the ball initially moving −3.60 m/s leaves at +2.00 m/s, taking the first ball's original direction as positive.

giancoli-ch7-q30.answer: Second ball's mass M = [(1 + 0.450)/(1 − 0.450)]m = 2.64m. Substitute the rebound velocity v₁′ = −0.450v₁ into v₁′/v₁ = (m − M)/(m + M).

giancoli-ch7-q32.answer: Fraction of the neutron's kinetic energy transferred to the target is 4mM/(m + M)²: (a) 1.00, or 100%; (b) 0.890, or 89.0%; (c) 0.286, or 28.6%; (d) 0.0192, or 1.92%. Use m = 1.01 u for the neutron and the stated target masses.

giancoli-ch7-q34.answer: (a) The fraction of kinetic energy lost in the sticking collision is M/(m + M); the retained fraction is m/(m + M). Momentum gives V = mv/(m + M), then compare ½(m + M)V² with ½mv². (b) The lost fraction is 380/(18.0 + 380) = 0.955, or 95.5%.

giancoli-ch7-q36.answer: The lighter piece receives 3300 J and the heavier piece 2200 J. Equal, opposite momenta imply inverse mass–energy proportionality: Klight/Kheavy = mheavy/mlight = 1.5, and their energies sum to 5500 J.

giancoli-ch7-q38.answer: Total net impulse during contact = m(vup + vdown) = 0.014[√(2g × 0.85) + √(2g × 1.5)] = 0.13 N·s upward. The floor's impulse is slightly larger by mgΔt; contact time is not provided.

giancoli-ch7-q40.answer: The lighter block travels nine times as far as the heavier: dlight/dheavy = 9. Equal, opposite momenta give vlight = 3vheavy; each block's frictional stopping deceleration is μkg, so stopping distance scales as v². Assume the same kinetic-friction coefficient.

giancoli-ch7-q42.answer: Minimum incident speed, in the limiting sense, is vmin = 2(M + m)√(gl)/m. Momentum during embedding gives V = mv/(M + m). The rigid rod can exert compression, so the threshold requires only enough energy to rise 2l: ½(M + m)V² = (M + m)g(2l). A speed just above the limiting value carries it over the top; the √(5gl) condition for a string does not apply.

giancoli-ch7-q44.answer: (a) x momentum: mAvA = mAvA′cos 30.0° + mBvB′cos θB. y momentum: 0 = mAvA′sin 30.0° + mBvB′sin θB. (b) Ball B's velocity components are (0.841, −0.900) m/s, giving speed 1.23 m/s at 46.9° below the original A direction. Its deflection is opposite A's transverse deflection.

giancoli-ch7-q46.answer: Ball A leaves along +x at 3.7 m/s; ball B leaves along +y at 2.0 m/s. Momentum gives vAx′ = 3.7 and vAy′ = 2.0 − vB′. Elastic energy conservation then gives vB′ = 2.0 m/s for the stated positive-y motion; the other algebraic root is vB′ = 0 and does not describe B moving along +y.

giancoli-ch7-q48.answer: Unknown atom mass ≈ 39.9 u, about 40 u. Momentum geometry gives vNe′/v₀ = sin 50.0°/sin 105.6° and (M/mNe)(vtarget′/v₀) = sin 55.6°/sin 105.6°. Substitute these into kinetic-energy conservation to obtain M = mNe sin²55.6°/[sin²105.6° − sin²50.0°].

giancoli-ch7-q52.answer: The center of mass lies at xCM = (23/6)l₀ = 3.83l₀ from the left face shown as x = 0. Masses are proportional to cube volumes 1:8:27, with centers at 0.5l₀, 2l₀, and 4.5l₀, so xCM/l₀ = (0.5 + 16 + 121.5)/36.

giancoli-ch7-q54.answer: Relative to the shown origin, (xCM,yCM) = (1.42 m, −0.251 m). Split into the full horizontal rectangle A, area 2.06 × 0.20 m² centered at (1.03, 0.10), and the nonoverlapping vertical rectangle B below the x axis, area 1.48 × 0.20 m² centered at (1.96, −0.74). Area-weight their centers; uniform density and thickness cancel.

giancoli-ch7-q56.answer: One complete leg, including its foot, has mass (21.5% + 9.6% + 3.4%)/2 = 17.25% of your total body mass. Thus mleg = 0.1725M; for example a 70-kg person has a representative leg mass of 12.1 kg. Use your own mass for a personal numerical value.

giancoli-ch7-q58.answer: For an upper arm horizontal to the right and the forearm/hand hanging vertically, the arm's CM is 21.7 cm to the right and 7.62 cm below the shoulder. From Table 7–1, shoulder-to-elbow = 0.190H, upper-arm CM = 0.095H from the shoulder, forearm CM = 0.069H below the elbow, and hand CM = 0.191H below it. Weight by masses 6.6:4.2:1.7 and use H = 155 cm. Rotating the whole pose rotates these CM coordinates.

giancoli-ch7-q60.answer: One defensible articulated-body estimate puts the CM about 0.056H below a horizontal torso median line, about 9.5 cm for height H = 1.70 m; it can therefore lie outside the body's outline.
steps: Take the torso and head horizontal, arms vertical, thighs sloping downward by 15° from the hip, and lower legs vertical. Table 7–1 then gives downward CM offset/H = 0.066(0.095) + 0.042(0.259) + 0.017(0.381) + 0.215(0.096 sin 15°) + 0.096(0.236 sin 15° + 0.103) + 0.034(0.236 sin 15° + 0.267) ≈ 0.0559.
assumptions: This is an estimate of a pose, not a uniquely dimensioned geometry: the 15° hip bend is assigned to the thighs while the torso stays horizontal. Distributing the bend between torso and thighs changes the numerical offset. Arms and lower legs hang vertically as in Problem 59.

giancoli-ch7-q62.answer: The center of mass is 25.1 cm above the bottom end of the handle, along the handle's axis toward the head. The handle's center is 12.0 cm from that end and the head's center is 24.0 + 4.00 = 28.0 cm away, so xCM = [0.500(12.0) + 2.30(28.0)]/2.80 = 25.1 cm. In free flight this point follows a parabola, neglecting air resistance.

giancoli-ch7-q64.answer: Measured from the original launch point: (a) part II lands at 7d/3 if mII = 3mI; (b) it lands at 5d if mI = 3mII. The CM would land at 2d as in Example 7–14, part I lands at d, and mId + mIIxII = (mI + mII)2d.

giancoli-ch7-q66.answer: The balloon rises at speed mv/(M + m) relative to Earth; the passenger moves downward at speed Mv/(M + m). Write VB − Vpassenger = v and MVB + mVpassenger = 0. When the passenger stops relative to the balloon, both return to zero speed, provided buoyancy continues balancing total weight and external drag is negligible.

giancoli-ch7-q68.answer: Combined asteroid velocity ≈ 0.20 km/s in A's original direction. Taking A positive, vf = [(7.5 × 10¹²)(3.3) − (1.45 × 10¹³)(1.4)]/(2.20 × 10¹³) = 0.202 km/s.

giancoli-ch7-q70.answer: Car speed after 60.0 min = m₀v₀/(m₀ + Δm) = 4800(7.60)/[4800 + 3.80(60.0)] = 7.26 m/s. Incoming snow has no horizontal momentum, so horizontal momentum is conserved while mass increases.

giancoli-ch7-q72.answer: Maximum rise = [mbvb/(M + mb)]²/(2g) = [0.0250(230)/1.425]²/(2 × 9.80) = 0.831 m. The embedding collision conserves momentum; the subsequent rise conserves mechanical energy, neglecting losses after embedding.

giancoli-ch7-q74.answer: (a) Earth recoils at v ≈ mvmeteor/ME = 6.3 × 10⁻¹³ m/s in the meteor's incoming direction. (b) Fraction of the meteor's energy transferred to Earth's translation ≈ m/ME = 2.5 × 10⁻¹⁷. (c) Earth's kinetic energy increases by about 1.2 J in the stated initially-rest frame. Nearly all the meteor's original kinetic energy becomes internal energy and other nontranslational forms.

giancoli-ch7-q76.answer: (a) Average barrier force = mΔv/Δt = 1.25 × 10⁵ N opposite the car's motion. (b) Average deceleration = (45/3.6)/0.15 = 83.3 m/s² = 8.5g.

giancoli-ch7-q78.answer: (a) Lighter ball's speed just before impact = √[2g(0.35)(1 − cos 66°)] = 2.02 m/s toward B. (b) After the elastic collision A rebounds at 0.367 m/s, and B moves forward at 1.65 m/s. (c) Their maximum rises above their respective lowest points are hA = vA′²/(2g) = 0.00686 m and hB = vB′²/(2g) = 0.139 m. Use the 45-g and 65-g masses in the one-dimensional elastic-collision formulas.

giancoli-ch7-q80.answer: (a) Shuttle recoil speed = msatellite(0.30)/(Mshuttle + msatellite) = 2.75 × 10⁻³ m/s in −x. (b) Average force on the satellite = msatellite[0.30Mshuttle/(Mshuttle + msatellite)]/4.8 = 52.6 N in +x. The stated 0.30 m/s is relative to the recoiling shuttle, so the satellite's velocity change in the initial common rest frame is slightly smaller.

giancoli-ch7-q82.answer: About 12 kg of gas must be ejected backward. The small-fuel-fraction momentum estimate is mgas ≈ MΔv/uexhaust = 210(2.0)/35 = 12 kg. If 35 m/s is the continuous exhaust speed relative to the changing spacecraft and 210 kg is initial total mass, the rocket equation gives the more exact value 210[1 − exp(−2.0/35)] = 11.7 kg, consistent with the estimate.

giancoli-ch7-q84.answer: The fourth bounce rises 4.00 m above the bottom level. Each perfectly elastic impact reverses the vertical velocity without reducing its magnitude, so the vertical-motion energy corresponding to the original elevation is retained. This assumes the ball hits the horizontal treads only and initially rolls off with zero vertical velocity.

giancoli-ch7-q86.answer: Yes: the ideal shot scratches into the upper-left corner pocket. To send the object ball to the upper-right pocket, its path has slope √3/3 and is 30° above horizontal. In an equal-mass elastic collision with a stationary target, the two outgoing velocities are perpendicular. Thus the cue ball travels at 120° to +x; from the impact point 1 unit from the left rail it rises √3 units before reaching that rail, exactly to the upper-left pocket.

giancoli-ch8-q2.answer: Solar radius ≈ d tan(0.25°) = 6.5 × 10⁸ m, or 6.5 × 10⁵ km. The stated 0.5° is the Sun's angular diameter, so halve it before computing the radius.

giancoli-ch8-q4.answer: Average angular acceleration = (0 − 6500 × 2π/60)/4.0 = −1.7 × 10² rad/s², opposite the initial rotation. This is also the instantaneous acceleration if the slowing is uniform.

giancoli-ch8-q6.answer: Ball diameter = distance/(π × revolutions) = 3.5/(12.0π) = 0.093 m, or 9.3 cm, assuming rolling without slipping.

giancoli-ch8-q8.answer: Each wheel makes N = 9200/[π(0.68)] ≈ 4.3 × 10³ revolutions, neglecting slip.

giancoli-ch8-q10.answer: (a) Linear speed = 2πr/T = 1.9 m/s. (b) Radial acceleration = 4π²r/T² = 3.0 m/s² inward; tangential acceleration = 0 for uniform rotation.

giancoli-ch8-q12.answer: (a) Orbital angular speed ≈ 2π/(365.25 × 86400) = 1.99 × 10⁻⁷ rad/s. (b) Spin angular speed ≈ 2π/86400 = 7.27 × 10⁻⁵ rad/s, or 7.29 × 10⁻⁵ rad/s using a sidereal day. Both angular-velocity vectors point approximately toward the north ecliptic/celestial poles respectively, by the right-hand rule.

giancoli-ch8-q14.answer: (a) α = [(280 − 120)2π/60]/4.0 = 4.2 rad/s². (b) At 2.0 s, speed is 200 rpm = 20.94 rad/s. Radial acceleration = ω²r = 134 m/s² inward; tangential acceleration = αr = 1.28 m/s² along the motion, with r = 0.305 m.

giancoli-ch8-q16.answer: For external contact without slipping, R₁ω₁ = −R₂ω₂ when the same angular sign convention is used. Thus ω₁/ω₂ = −R₂/R₁; their angular-speed magnitudes have ratio R₂/R₁. The turntable and roller rotate in opposite directions.

giancoli-ch8-q18.answer: The centrifuge turns 3.00 × 10⁴ revolutions. With uniform acceleration from rest, average rotation rate is 7500 rpm, and 240 s is 4.00 min.

giancoli-ch8-q20.answer: (a) α = −ω₀²/(2Δθ) = −0.504 rad/s², where ω₀ = 850(2π/60) rad/s and Δθ = 1250(2π) rad. (b) Stopping time = −ω₀/α = 176 s, about 2.94 min.

giancoli-ch8-q22.answer: (a) Angular acceleration ≈ −3.07 rad/s², with the initial rolling rotation positive. Use ω = v/0.40 and Δθ = 75(2π). (b) From 55 km/h the additional stopping time is 12.4 s. (c) The additional distance is 95.0 m; the corresponding linear deceleration is 1.23 m/s².

giancoli-ch8-q24.answer: (a) Maximum torque = mgr = 52(9.80)(0.17) = 87 N·m, when the crank arm is horizontal. (b) Increase the force beyond body weight by pulling on the handlebars/other pedal if possible, or use a longer crank arm; both increase the available moment arm or force.

giancoli-ch8-q26.answer: (a) Torque magnitude = Fr = 42(0.96) = 40 N·m. (b) At 60.0° to the door face, τ = Fr sin 60.0° = 35 N·m. These assume the hinge axis lies at the opposite edge.

giancoli-ch8-q28.answer: Required hand force = τ/L = 95/0.28 = 3.4 × 10² N. The force at each of six equally loaded bolt contacts is of order 2 × 10³ N: treating 15 mm as the across-flats dimension gives vertex radius 15/√3 = 8.66 mm and tangential contact force 95/(6 × 0.00866) = 1.83 kN per point. This is an idealized equal-load estimate; actual wrench contacts need not share equally.

giancoli-ch8-q30.answer: For a uniform solid sphere, I = (2/5)MR² = (2/5)(10.8)(0.648)² = 1.81 kg·m². A hollow shell would have a different inertia.

giancoli-ch8-q32.answer: Required net torque = Iα = ½MR²(Δω/Δt) = ½(31000)(7.0)²(0.68/34) = 1.52 × 10⁴ N·m, about 1.5 × 10⁴ N·m.

giancoli-ch8-q34.answer: (a) I = ½MR² = 1.37 × 10⁻³ kg·m². (b) Applied torque = I(αdesired + |αfriction|) = 0.0542 N·m. Here αdesired = (1750 × 2π/60)/5.00 and |αfriction| = (1500 × 2π/60)/55.0; assume the measured friction torque remains constant.

giancoli-ch8-q36.answer: (a) α = v/(Lt) = 8.5/(0.31 × 0.38) = 72 rad/s². (b) In the simplified rotational model, muscle force ≈ [mballL² + marmL²/3]α/(0.025 m) = 6.2 × 10² N. This treats 31 cm as elbow-to-ball distance and neglects the varying gravitational torque; including gravity would require the arm's orientation throughout the throw.

giancoli-ch8-q38.answer: (a) I = mr² = 0.350(1.2)² = 0.50 kg·m². (b) Required driving torque = Fairr = 0.020(1.2) = 0.024 N·m in the direction of rotation, balancing drag at constant angular speed.

giancoli-ch8-q40.answer: (a) Hand torque magnitude = Fr = 1.5(0.045) = 0.068 N·m, opposite the rotation. (b) With only this torque, stopping time = Iω₀/τ = 0.11(1.6 × 2π)/0.0675 = 16 s.

giancoli-ch8-q42.answer: Mass ≈ 23.3 kg. Uniform acceleration from rest gives α = 2Δθ/t² = 2(160 × 2π)/15.0². Using τ = Iα and I = (2/5)M(0.36)² yields the mass.

giancoli-ch8-q44.answer: The rotor takes 6.27 s to stop and turns 481 revolutions. Use I = ½(3.10)(0.0710)², α = −1.20/I, ω₀ = 9200(2π/60), t = −ω₀/α, and Δθ = ω₀t/2.

giancoli-ch8-q46.answer: (a) Each block has gravity, a normal force perpendicular to its incline, and tension toward the pulley. The pulley has the two tangential string forces and an axle reaction. (b) TA = mA(a + g sin 32°) = 49.5 N; TB = mB(g sin 61° − a) = 75.7 N. (c) Net pulley torque = (TB − TA)R = 3.93 N·m clockwise. Since α = a/R, I = (TB − TA)R²/a = 0.589 kg·m². Assume no bearing-friction torque.

giancoli-ch8-q48.answer: (a) Angular acceleration = (v/r)²/[2(4 × 2π)] = 9.70 rad/s². (b) Tangential acceleration = rα = 11.6 m/s². (c) Centripetal acceleration just before release = v²/r = 585 m/s². (d) Athlete's net force ≈ m√(ar² + atan²) = 4.27 × 10³ N. (e) It is 1.14° from the inward radial direction toward the forward tangent. Gravity is excluded as directed.

giancoli-ch8-q52.answer: Total kinetic energy = ½mv² + ½(2mr²/5)(v/r)² = (7/10)mv² = 48.8 J. This models the bowling ball as a uniform solid sphere rolling without slipping.

giancoli-ch8-q54.answer: Required steady motor power ≈ 1.19 × 10⁵ W = 159 hp, about 160 hp. From the uniform spin-down, the resisting torque is Iω/16; at the original speed its power loss is Iω²/16. Use I = ½(220)(5.5)² and ω = 3.8(2π). Assume this resistance torque is unchanged during powered operation.

giancoli-ch8-q56.answer: (a) For a uniform solid sphere, v = √[(10/7)gL sin 30°] = 8.37 m/s and ω = v/r = 24.3 rad/s. (b) Ktrans/Krot = 5/2 = 2.50. (c) Linear speed and the energy ratio depend on neither mass nor radius; angular speed depends on radius as 1/r, and none of these results depends on mass. Rolling is without slipping.

giancoli-ch8-q58.answer: Speed just before mB strikes the ground ≈ 2.03 m/s. Energy gives (mB − mA)gh = ½[mA + mB + I/R²]v² with I/R² = Mpulley/2 = 1.55 kg and h = 2.5 m. The pulley radius cancels for a uniform cylinder.

giancoli-ch8-q60.answer: Angular momentum magnitude = mr²ω = 0.270(1.35)²(10.4) = 5.12 kg·m²/s. Its direction is perpendicular to the orbital plane, given by the right-hand rule.

giancoli-ch8-q62.answer: (a) Raising the arms increases the total moment of inertia; with negligible external torque, angular momentum Iω is conserved, so rotation slows. (b) Iafter/Ibefore = 0.90/0.60 = 1.50 for the person-plus-platform system. If the platform has nonnegligible inertia, the person's individual inertia ratio requires that inertia separately.

giancoli-ch8-q64.answer: Straight-position rotation rate = (2.0/1.5)/3.5 = 0.38 rev/s. Tucking reduces inertia by 3.5 and increases angular speed by the same factor when angular momentum is conserved.

giancoli-ch8-q66.answer: (a) Angular momentum = Iω = ½(48)(0.15)²(3.0 × 2π) = 10.2 kg·m²/s. (b) Average braking torque = −L/4.0 = −2.54 N·m, opposite the spin, with arms fixed.

giancoli-ch8-q68.answer: Final frequency ≈ 1.41 rev/s. Angular momentum gives ff = fiIwheel/(Iwheel + Iclay), with Iwheel = ½(5.0)(0.20)² = 0.100 kg·m² and Iclay = ½(2.6)(0.070)² = 0.00637 kg·m². Assume the clay initially has negligible angular momentum about the wheel axis and remains centered.

giancoli-ch8-q70.answer: Angular momentum about the vertical central axis is L = [Ml²/12 + 2m(l/2)²]ω = (M/12 + m/2)l²ω, in the direction of the angular-velocity vector. Treat the end masses as points.

giancoli-ch8-q72.answer: Final rotation frequency = (3/5)(3.3) = 1.98 rev/s, about 2.0 rev/s. The disk has I = MR²/2 and the centered rod of length 2R has I = M(2R)²/12 = MR²/3. Conserve total angular momentum during contact.

giancoli-ch8-q74.answer: Turntable angular speed = 0.305 rad/s opposite the runner, about 2.92 rpm. Let the person's speed relative to the turntable be u = 4.0 m/s; conservation gives Iωtable + mr²(ωtable + u/r) = 0. Thus ωtable = −mru/(I + mr²), with r = 2.75 m. The person's ground speed is not 4.0 m/s.

giancoli-ch8-q76.answer: Motor torque ≈ Iα = ½(1.6)(0.20)²(24 × 2π/6.0) = 0.80 N·m, assuming no resisting torque.

giancoli-ch8-q78.answer: (a) Speed just before the string ends ≈ 1.08 m/s. Use M = 0.105 kg, hub radius b = 0.0065 m, and I = 2[½(0.050)(0.0375)²] + ½(0.0050)(0.0065)². Then Mgh = ½(M + I/b²)v² with h = 1.0 m. (b) Rotational fraction = (I/b²)/(M + I/b²) = 0.941, or 94.1%. Assume no slip between string and hub.

giancoli-ch8-q80.answer: Required average torque = IΔω/Δt = (0.60)(1.5)²(75 × 2π/60)/5.0 = 2.1 N·m. It comes from David moving his hand so the sling force has a tangential component while the rock accelerates; a force directed exactly toward a fixed center supplies no torque about that center.

giancoli-ch8-q82.answer: (a) Iperpendicular = 2mHr² ≈ 3.1 × 10⁻⁴⁷ kg·m². (b) For the in-plane bisector, I = 2mHr²sin²52° ≈ 1.9 × 10⁻⁴⁷ kg·m². The oxygen atom lies on each specified axis and contributes zero in the point-atom model; use mH ≈ 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg and r = 0.096 nm.

giancoli-ch8-q84.answer: (a) Earth spin angular momentum ≈ 7.1 × 10³³ kg·m²/s using I = (2/5)MER E² and a 24-h day. (b) Orbital angular momentum ≈ 2.7 × 10⁴⁰ kg·m²/s using L = MErorbit²(2π/year), rorbit ≈ 1.50 × 10¹¹ m. Directions follow the spin and orbital right-hand rules respectively.

giancoli-ch8-q86.answer: The static-friction threshold torque is μs(mg/4)R = 0.65(1080 × 9.80/4)(0.33) = 5.7 × 10² N·m per driven tire. A torque just above the threshold causes slipping in the simplified model. Wheel rotational inertia and dynamic weight transfer are neglected; they would modify the exact applied axle-torque threshold.

giancoli-ch8-q88.answer: Final speed = r₁v₁/r₂ = (0.80)(2.4)/0.48 = 4.0 m/s. The string exerts no torque about the hole, so angular momentum mrv is conserved. Kinetic energy increases because pulling the string does positive work.

giancoli-ch8-q90.answer: Using solar radius 6.96 × 10⁸ m and neutron-star radius 1.2 × 10⁴ m: (a) if the lost mass carries no angular momentum, ffinal = 4(Rinitial/Rfinal)²finitial ≈ 1.7 × 10⁴ rev/s. (b) If it carries away 3/4 of the initial angular momentum, ffinal = (Rinitial/Rfinal)²finitial ≈ 4.3 × 10³ rev/s. These follow the stipulated uniform-sphere, angular-momentum model; the initial mass cancels.

giancoli-ch8-q92.answer: Ratio Lspin/Lorbit = (2/5)(RMoon/rorbit)² ≈ 8.2 × 10⁻⁶, treating the Moon as a uniform sphere. Its synchronous rotation means the spin and orbital angular speeds are equal, so they cancel from the ratio.

giancoli-ch8-q94.answer: In the stipulated uniform-Sun, circular-orbit model, the four outer planets possess about 96.5% of total angular momentum. Their summed orbital momentum is Σ[mi ri²(2π/Ti)] ≈ 3.12 × 10⁴³ kg·m²/s; Sun spin is (2/5)MSRS²(2π/25 days) ≈ 1.12 × 10⁴² kg·m²/s. The planetary fraction is Lplanets/(Lplanets + LSun).

giancoli-ch8-q96.answer: (a) Paper unrolled while pulling ≈ 3.04 m. Net torque = FR − τfr = 3.5(0.076) − 0.11 = 0.156 N·m, so α = 47.3 rad/s² and length = Rαt²/2. (b) Additional coast-down length ≈ 4.31 m, from R[Iω²/(2τfr)] with ω = α(1.3 s). Assume the roll starts from rest and its radius and inertia stay constant as specified.

giancoli-ch9-q2.answer: Required hanging mass = (15.0 kg)(0.350 m)/(0.780 m) = 6.73 kg. Balance torques about the hip: tension × 0.780 = leg weight × 0.350, with an ideal pulley giving tension = mg.

giancoli-ch9-q4.answer: Diver mass = τ/(gd) = 1800/[9.80(1.0 + 3.0)] = 45.9 kg, about 46 kg. The lever arm from A to the diver is the full 4.0 m.

giancoli-ch9-q6.answer: Each jaw exerts about 34.6 N on the rod. Torque balance about pivot P for either arm gives Fjaw(2.70 cm) = 11.0 N(8.50 cm). The equal and opposite clamping forces do not add to a net force on the rod; their combined inward load magnitude is 69.3 N.

giancoli-ch9-q8.answer: Required downward pull equals rope tension: (a) 225 N; (b) 2.05 × 10³ N. With half-span 3.3 m and sag y, 2T[y/√(3.3² + y²)] = mg. Reducing sag greatly increases tension.

giancoli-ch9-q10.answer: FA = 2.94 × 10³ N downward; FB = 1.47 × 10⁴ N upward. Figure 9–9 has the beam's center 25 m from A and B 20 m from A, so FB(20) = mg(25) and FA + FB = mg with upward positive. The negative algebraic FA means A must pull downward.

giancoli-ch9-q12.answer: Sloping-cord tension = mg/sin 33° = 3.42 × 10³ N. Horizontal-cord tension = mg cot 33° = 2.87 × 10³ N. Vertical and horizontal force balances at the knot determine them.

giancoli-ch9-q14.answer: The person's center of mass must remain at least 0.282 m inward from the tabletop edge. Taking moments about the nearer leg at impending tipping, 66.0g d = 24.0g(0.600), so the person's permissible distance outside that leg is 0.218 m; subtract from the 0.500-m overhang. This models the seated person as a point weight at the seat location.

giancoli-ch9-q16.answer: FA = 6.27 × 10³ N upward and FB = 6.07 × 10³ N upward. With A at x = 0 and B at x = 10.0 m, FB(10) = 4300(2) + 3100(6) + 2200(9) + (280g)(5). Vertical force balance gives FA.

giancoli-ch9-q18.answer: Wire tension = 642 N; hinge force is 526 N to the right and 1.67 N upward. Torque balance gives T sin 35°(1.35) = 215(1.70) + 155(0.850). Then Hx = T cos 35° and Hy = 215 + 155 − T sin 35°. The small vertical hinge component results from the near cancellation of loads.

giancoli-ch9-q20.answer: Left support force = (7/8)Mg = 8.06 × 10³ N; right = (5/8)Mg = 5.76 × 10³ N, both upward. The full beam acts at l/2 and the half-beam at l/4, giving right-support torque RB l = Mg(l/2) + (Mg/2)(l/4).

giancoli-ch9-q22.answer: (a) Maximum person weight is 650 N. At impending tipping about B, the beam's weight 650 N acts 5.0 m left of B and the person 5.0 m right. (b) At D with that limiting person, A exerts 0 and B 1300 N upward. (c) With that same person 2.0 m right of A, A exerts 812.5 N and B 487.5 N upward, from RB(12) = 650(7) + 650(2).

giancoli-ch9-q24.answer: The person's CG is 0.905 m from the bottom of her feet. Taking moments about the feet gives total weight × xCG = head-scale force × 1.72 m, so xCG = 1.72(35.1)/(35.1 + 31.6).

giancoli-ch9-q26.answer: Net tension ≈ 121 N. Each wire's horizontal component is 115(2.0)/√(2.0² + 2.6²) N. The two ground anchors and pole base form an equilateral triangle, so these components make 60° with each other; their resultant is 2Fhorizontal cos 30°, balanced by the horizontal net tension.

giancoli-ch9-q28.answer: The nails must exert at least 2.35 × 10³ N downward. Take moments about the support 0.75 m from A: Fnails(0.75) = (65g)(3.0 − 0.75) + (45g)(1.5 − 0.75).

giancoli-ch9-q30.answer: Minimum angle is θmin = arctan[1/(2μs)]. The frictionless wall exerts horizontal Nwall; torque balance about the foot gives Nwall l sin θ = mg(l/2)cos θ. Ground normal is mg and required friction equals Nwall, so ½mg cot θ ≤ μsmg. Thus tan θ ≥ 1/(2μs).

giancoli-ch9-q32.answer: Required extensor force ≈ 9.7 × 10² N. Balance moments about the elbow: FM(0.025) = (7.3g)(0.300) + (2.3g)(0.120), using the perpendicular moment arms shown.

giancoli-ch9-q34.answer: (a) Muscle force = mg(0.24)/[0.12 sin 15°] = 250 N. (b) Shoulder-joint force magnitude ≈ 244 N, directed 7.63° below horizontal toward the hand. Its components are (FM cos 15°, mg − FM sin 15°) = (241, −32.3) N, balancing the arm's weight and muscle pull.

giancoli-ch9-q36.answer: Achilles-tendon tension ≈ 1.41 × 10³ N upward; lower-leg-bone force ≈ 2.12 × 10³ N downward. The ground normal is mg. Taking moments about the toe pivot gives FB D = FT(D + d), and vertical balance gives FB = FT + mg. With D = 2d, FT = 2mg and FB = 3mg. Neglect the foot's own weight.

giancoli-ch9-q38.answer: Yes, the idealized tower is stable: its CG is displaced only 4.5/2 = 2.25 m from the base center, within the 7.7-m radius. The limiting top displacement is about 2(7.7) = 15.4 m, so the top could lean about 10.9 m farther in this simple uniform-tower model. Foundation failure and actual structural limits are excluded.

giancoli-ch9-q40.answer: Extension ≈ FL/(EA) = 275(0.300)/[3 × 10⁹ × π(0.00100)²/4] = 0.035 m, or 3.5 cm. Use the book's approximate nylon Young modulus E ≈ 3 × 10⁹ Pa; the linear-elastic estimate is correspondingly approximate.

giancoli-ch9-q42.answer: Column shortening ≈ FL/(EA) = (25000g)(8.6)/[(50 × 10⁹)(1.4)] = 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ m, or 0.030 mm. This uses the load and area from Problem 41 and marble E = 50 GPa, ignoring the column's own weight.

giancoli-ch9-q44.answer: Final volume ≈ 997.5 cm³, about 997 cm³. With alcohol bulk modulus B ≈ 1.0 × 10⁹ Pa, ΔV = −V₀ΔP/B. From atmospheric pressure to 2.6 × 10⁶ Pa, ΔP ≈ 2.5 × 10⁶ Pa and volume loss ≈ 2.5 cm³; ignoring atmospheric pressure gives 997.4 cm³, essentially the same estimate.

giancoli-ch9-q48.answer: The iron bathysphere's material volume contracts by about 0.022%. With iron bulk modulus B = 90 GPa, |ΔV|/V = ΔP/B ≈ (2.0 × 10⁷)/(9.0 × 10¹⁰). This is the book's bulk-compression estimate; a hollow shell's exact interior-volume change would also depend on its geometry and thickness.

giancoli-ch9-q50.answer: Ideal ultimate compressive force = σultimate A = (170 × 10⁶)(3.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 5.1 × 10⁴ N, using the bone value in Table 9–2. This is an ideal material-strength estimate, not a clinical safe-load threshold.

giancoli-ch9-q52.answer: (a) It does not break under the book's simple compressive-strength test: stress = 3.3 × 10⁴/(3.6 × 10⁻⁴) = 9.17 × 10⁷ Pa, below 1.70 × 10⁸ Pa. (b) With bone E = 15 GPa, shortening = FL/(EA) = 1.34 mm. Real bone loading also depends on geometry, bending, and other factors.

giancoli-ch9-q54.answer: Minimum area of support A ≈ 1.60 × 10⁻³ m² (16.0 cm²), and support B ≈ 9.14 × 10⁻³ m² (91.4 cm²). Equilibrium gives A pulling downward with 0.25mg and B pushing upward with 1.25mg. Apply safety factor 9 using wood's parallel-grain tensile strength 40 MPa for A and compressive strength 35 MPa for B; A must be anchored to carry tension.

giancoli-ch9-q56.answer: Required diameter ≈ 2.71 cm. Maximum cable tension = m(g + a) = 3100(9.80 + 1.8) N. With safety factor 8 and steel ultimate tensile strength 500 MPa, A ≥ 8T/σultimate, giving d ≥ √(4A/π) = 0.0271 m.

giancoli-ch9-q58.answer: Ring-segment tension = 420000/[2 sin 5°] = 2.41 × 10⁶ N. The two nearly opposing segment tensions each contribute F sin 5° toward the required radial resultant.

giancoli-ch9-q60.answer: (a) Sliding occurs first if μs < l/(2h). (b) Tipping occurs first if μs > l/(2h); equality makes the ideal thresholds coincide. Sliding starts at Fslide = μsmg. At tipping, the normal force acts at the downstream bottom edge and torque balance gives Ftip h = mg(l/2). Compare these two threshold forces.

giancoli-ch9-q62.answer: Limiting side-slope angle ≈ arctan[(2.4/2)/2.2] = 28.6°. The CG's vertical projection must remain within the downhill tire contact edge. This neglects sliding and suspension motion; the 4.0-m overall height is not the CG height.

giancoli-ch9-q64.answer: Using the base compressive-stress limit, hmax = σcompressive/(ρg): (a) steel ≈ 6.5 km; (b) granite ≈ 6.4 km. Area cancels because both self-weight ρAhg and load-carrying capacity σA scale with A. Strictly this is a crushing limit, not an Euler-buckling limit; actual slender-column buckling depends on cross-sectional geometry and can occur much earlier.

giancoli-ch9-q66.answer: Both extreme ends are unsafe. With x measured from the left end, the painter must stay between x = 0.169 m and x = 5.954 m: at least 17 cm from the left end and 4.6 cm from the right. The supports are at x = 1 and 5 m, scaffold CG at 3 m, and pail at 2 m. Require the combined CM [65x + 25(3) + 4(2)]/94 to stay between the supports; the limiting case has zero tension in the farther rope.

giancoli-ch9-q68.answer: At least 7 vertical supports on each 10.0-m side, 14 total. One support's safe compressive load is (35 MPa)(0.040 × 0.090)/12 = 10500 N; half the roof weighs 13600g/2 = 66640 N, needing ceil(66640/10500) = 7 supports per side. If end supports are placed at both corners, equal spacing is 10.0/(7 − 1) = 1.67 m. This assumes equal load sharing and compression parallel to the wood grain, ignoring buckling as directed.

giancoli-ch9-q70.answer: Bear's downward force ≈ 565 N. Initially 2T₀ sin 15° = mg; afterward 2(2T₀)sin 27° = mg + Fbear. Eliminate T₀ to obtain Fbear = mg[2 sin 27°/sin 15° − 1], with m = 23.0 kg.

giancoli-ch9-q72.answer: (a) Fractional shortening = F/(EA) = 65g/[200 × 10⁹ × π(0.15)²] = 4.51 × 10⁻⁸, or 4.51 × 10⁻⁶%. (b) Interatomic spacing decreases by the same fraction, giving Δd ≈ (2.0 × 10⁻¹⁰)(4.51 × 10⁻⁸) = 9.0 × 10⁻¹⁸ m. Use steel E = 200 GPa and ignore the rod's self-weight.

giancoli-ch9-q74.answer: Sliding threshold force = μsW = 0.60(250) = 150 N horizontally. To avoid tipping before sliding, h ≤ W(b/2)/F = 250(0.50)/150 = 0.833 m. A force just above 150 N starts sliding when applied below this limiting height; at equality, tipping and sliding thresholds coincide.

giancoli-ch9-q76.answer: The average contact stress is about 3.8 × 10⁵ Pa, below the stated 5 × 10⁵ Pa ultimate tissue strength. Stopping over 1.0 m requires equivalent net force mv²/(2d) = 1.13 × 10⁵ N, and the upward snow force is this plus mg. Divide by 0.30 m² to get the stress. Thus the supplied simple average-stress model permits survival; it does not establish safety for real impacts or peak/local stresses.

giancoli-ch9-q78.answer: Masses: A = 0.249 kg, C = 0.194 kg, D = 0.0554 kg. Bottom-bar balance gives 17.50mD = 5.00mC, hence mC = 3.5mD. Middle-bar balance gives 15.00(mC + mD) = 5.00(0.748), so mC + mD = 0.2493 kg. Top-bar balance gives 30.00mA = 7.50(0.748 + mC + mD).

giancoli-ch9-q80.answer: (a) Draw shelf weight downward at its midpoint, the upper slot's downward contact at the inserted left tip, and the lower slot's upward contact at the wall face 2.0 cm to its right. Two contact forces are needed to resist rotation as well as support weight. (b) Weight = 64.7 N; upward contact = 550 N; downward contact = 485 N. The shelf's full length is 32.0 + 2.0 = 34.0 cm, so its CG is 17.0 cm from the left tip. (c) Support torque about that tip is +11.0 N·m, counterclockwise, balancing the weight's clockwise torque.

giancoli-ch10-q2.answer: Air mass ≈ ρV = 1.29(5.6)(3.6)(2.4) = 62 kg, using the book's air density of 1.29 kg/m³. Actual room-temperature density can be somewhat lower.

giancoli-ch10-q4.answer: For your mass M in kg, estimated body volume is V ≈ M/1000 m³ = M liters, because mean human-body density is near that of water. For example, 70 kg corresponds to about 0.070 m³ or 70 L. This is a sample estimate, not an assertion of your actual mass.

giancoli-ch10-q6.answer: Mixture specific gravity = (0.80 × 4.0 + 1.00 × 5.0)/9.0 = 0.91. Masses add and the question specifies that the final volume is 9.0 L.

giancoli-ch10-q8.answer: Required pressure difference ≈ ρgh = 1000(9.80)(46) = 4.5 × 10⁵ Pa, about 4.5 atm above the pressure at the top. This is a hydrostatic column estimate, not a full model of water transport in a tree.

giancoli-ch10-q10.answer: Pressure at the feet is about 135 mm-Hg greater than at the head. Use ΔP = ρbloodgh and convert by ρHg g: ΔhHg = (1050/13600)(1.75 m) = 0.135 m. This is the hydrostatic contribution.

giancoli-ch10-q12.answer: Alcohol-column height ≈ Patm/(ρg) = 1.013 × 10⁵/(790 × 9.80) = 13.1 m, assuming negligible vapor pressure above the column.

giancoli-ch10-q14.answer: Maximum vehicle mass ≈ PgaugeA/g = [17.0(1.013 × 10⁵)]π(0.255)²/(4g) = 8.97 × 10³ kg. This excludes the lift platform's mass and losses; the stated output-line diameter is taken as the effective output-piston diameter.

giancoli-ch10-q16.answer: (a) Bottom absolute pressure = Patm + ρgh ≈ 1.19 × 10⁵ Pa. The total downward force from this pressure on the 238-m² bottom is about 2.83 × 10⁷ N; its gauge-pressure contribution is 4.20 × 10⁶ N. (b) Near the bottom, the side pressure is the same 1.19 × 10⁵ Pa absolute, or 1.76 × 10⁴ Pa gauge, because hydrostatic pressure at a given depth is direction-independent.

giancoli-ch10-q18.answer: Oil density ≈ 683 kg/m³. At the interface level, equal pressures give ρoil(27.2 cm) = ρwater(27.2 − 8.62 cm), since the right water surface is 8.62 cm below the oil surface. Points a and b are at equal depth in connected stationary water.

giancoli-ch10-q20.answer: Minimum gauge pressure = ρgh = 1000(9.80)(44) = 4.3 × 10⁵ Pa. This is the limiting zero-flow value; finite outlet speed and pipe losses require additional pressure.

giancoli-ch10-q22.answer: (a) Absolute tank pressure = 104000 + 13600g(0.185) = 1.287 × 10⁵ Pa. (b) Absolute tank pressure = 104000 − 13600g(0.056) = 9.65 × 10⁴ Pa. An open-arm mercury level above the tank-side level indicates tank pressure above atmospheric.

giancoli-ch10-q24.answer: Rock density = ρwater m/(m − mapparent) = 1000(9.28)/(9.28 − 6.18) = 2.99 × 10³ kg/m³. The displaced-water mass is 3.10 kg.

giancoli-ch10-q26.answer: Maximum cargo mass ≈ (ρair − ρHe)(4πr³/3) − mstructure = (1.29 − 0.179)(4π × 7.15³/3) − 930 = 771 kg. This is the neutral-buoyancy limit under the book's gas-density values.

giancoli-ch10-q28.answer: True mass ≈ mapparent/(1 − ρair/ρAl) = 4.0000/[1 − 1.29/2700] = 4.0019 kg. This interprets apparent mass as apparent weight divided by g; a real balance calibrated with buoyant reference weights requires their density as well.

giancoli-ch10-q30.answer: (a) Buoyant force = ρseawaterVg = 1025(0.0696)(9.80) = 699 N. (b) She sinks because total weight = 72.8g = 713 N, exceeding buoyancy by about 14 N. Assume the stated volume is maintained.

giancoli-ch10-q32.answer: (a) Liquid density = ρAl(m − mapparent)/m = 2700(3.80 − 2.10)/3.80 = 1.21 × 10³ kg/m³. (b) Generally, ρliquid = ρsolid(m − mapparent)/m for a fully submerged solid, neglecting air buoyancy and suspension forces other than the scale reading.

giancoli-ch10-q34.answer: (a) Buoyancy = ρseawaterg(4π × 2.60³/3) = 7.40 × 10⁵ N upward. (b) Cable tension = buoyancy − mg = 1.04 × 10⁴ N, pulling the chamber downward. Use seawater density 1025 kg/m³.

giancoli-ch10-q36.answer: Volumes add: V = fm/0.90 + (1 − f)m/1.10 when densities are in g/cm³. Dividing by m and using body density X g/cm³ gives 1/X = f/0.90 + (1 − f)/1.10. Solving, f = 4.95/X − 4.50, hence percent body fat = 495/X − 450. This follows only the stated two-component model.

giancoli-ch10-q38.answer: About 3.4 × 10³ balloons, or at least 3445 under the ideal numerical assumptions. Each 33-cm-diameter sphere displaces 4π(0.165)³/3 m³ and has net lifting capacity (1.29 − 0.179)V ≈ 0.0209 kg. Divide 72 kg by that value. Balloon skins, strings, and actual gas conditions increase the real requirement.

giancoli-ch10-q40.answer: Limiting lead mass ≈ 4.0 kg. With the wood just fully submerged, excess buoyancy is 3.65g because its SG is 0.50. The lead's effective submerged weight is mleadg(1 − ρwater/ρlead). Thus mlead = 3.65/(1 − 1000/11300) = 4.004 kg; a slightly larger mass causes sinking.

giancoli-ch10-q42.answer: Average artery flow speed ≈ 0.90 m/s. Example 10–12 gives aortic radius 1.2 cm and speed 0.40 m/s, hence Q = π(0.012)²(0.40). Divide by the stipulated combined artery area 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ m².

giancoli-ch10-q44.answer: With v₁ = v₂ = 0, Bernoulli's equation becomes P₁ + ρgy₁ = P₂ + ρgy₂. Therefore P₂ − P₁ = ρg(y₁ − y₂): moving downward a depth h increases pressure by ρgh, the hydrostatic relation.

giancoli-ch10-q46.answer: Input-tube speed = Q/A = [0.36(1.0)(0.60)/(3.0 × 3600)]/[π(0.030)²/4] = 0.028 m/s, or 2.8 cm/s. Assume the tank is filled to the stated height.

giancoli-ch10-q48.answer: Filling time ≈ 5.17 × 10⁵ s = 144 h, about 6.0 days. Divide pool volume π(6.1)²(1.4)/4 by hose flow Q = π[(5/8)(0.0254)]²(0.40)/4, with no leakage and the stated unusually low hose speed maintained.

giancoli-ch10-q50.answer: Volume flow ≈ 8.98 × 10⁻³ m³/s, or 9.0 L/s. Continuity gives v₂ = (6.0/4.5)²v₁; horizontal Bernoulli gives 33500 − 22600 = ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²), yielding v₁ = 3.18 m/s. Then Q = π(0.060)²v₁/4.

giancoli-ch10-q52.answer: Ideal Bernoulli lift ≈ ½ρair(vtop² − vbottom²)A = ½(1.29)(280² − 150²)(88) = 3.17 × 10⁶ N upward. This uses the prescribed flow speeds and treats the pressure difference as uniform over the area.

giancoli-ch10-q54.answer: Over a small displacement dx, net pressure work is (P₁A − P₂A)dx = (P₁ − P₂)dV. Dividing by dt gives power = (P₁ − P₂)(dV/dt) = (P₁ − P₂)Q. For inviscid steady flow this pressure work must be balanced by kinetic or potential energy changes; in a horizontal uniform pipe with equal end speeds, Bernoulli implies no sustained pressure drop.

giancoli-ch10-q55.answer: Continuity gives v₂ = (A₁/A₂)v₁. Bernoulli between the open top and outlet, both at atmospheric pressure, gives ½(v₁² − v₂²) = g(y₂ − y₁) = gh. Substitute continuity: v₁²[1 − (A₁/A₂)²] = 2gh, so v₁ = √{2gh/[1 − A₁²/A₂²]}. The nearly steady approximation is appropriate for A₁ much smaller than A₂.

giancoli-ch10-q56.answer: (a) Use A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ and P₁ − P₂ = ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²) to obtain v₁ = A₂√{2(P₁ − P₂)/[ρ(A₁² − A₂²)]}. (b) With diameters 3.5 cm and 1.0 cm and ΔP = 18 mm-Hg ≈ 2400 Pa, main-pipe speed is 0.179 m/s and the throat speed is 2.20 m/s. These two speeds differ by area ratio (3.5/1.0)² = 12.25.

giancoli-ch10-q58.answer: Viscosity ≈ 0.080 Pa·s using the narrow-gap model. With gap b = 0.0020 m, inner radius r = 0.0510 m, wetted length L = 0.120 m, and ω = 57(2π/60), τ = η(ωr/b)(2πrL)r. Thus η = τb/(2πLωr³). Ignore end effects; the exact concentric-cylinder solution gives about 0.076 Pa·s, close to this gap approximation.

giancoli-ch10-q60.answer: The watering time is reduced by a factor (5/3)⁴ = 7.72, becoming 12.96% of its former value. This uses Poiseuille flow with fixed pressure difference, length, and viscosity, for which Q ∝ diameter⁴; real turbulent garden-hose flow need not obey this scaling.

giancoli-ch10-q62.answer: Required pressure difference ≈ 8ηLQ/(πr⁴) = 8(0.20)(1600)(650 × 10⁻⁶)/[π(0.145)⁴] = 1.20 × 10³ Pa. This is the horizontal laminar-flow estimate; elevation changes would add a hydrostatic term.

giancoli-ch10-q64.answer: New vessel radius = (0.35)^(1/4)rold = 0.769rold, a decrease of 23.1%. Equivalently it is smaller by a factor 1/0.769 = 1.30, since fixed pressure gradient gives flow proportional to r⁴.

giancoli-ch10-q66.answer: Bottle height ≈ 1.04 m above the needle. Hydrostatic pressure must cover vein pressure plus viscous needle loss: ρgh = 78(133.322 Pa) + 8ηLQ/(πr⁴). Use ρ = 1050 kg/m³, η ≈ 4 × 10⁻³ Pa·s, L = 0.025 m, r = 0.00040 m, and Q = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶/60 m³/s. Ignore resistance of the wider tube.

giancoli-ch10-q68.answer: Required force = 2γL = 2(0.025)(0.215) = 0.0108 N. The factor of two counts the soap film's two surfaces.

giancoli-ch10-q70.answer: Not under the stated circular-contact model. Maximum surface-tension support is 6(2πrγ) ≈ 8.3 × 10⁻⁵ N, while the insect weighs 1.57 × 10⁻⁴ N. Thus the available support is only about 53% of its weight. Actual insects may have much longer effective contact lines or other support contributions.

giancoli-ch10-q72.answer: The calf reading would overestimate heart-level pressure by ΔP ≈ ρbloodg(1 m) = 1.03 × 10⁴ Pa, about 77 mm-Hg. This is the hydrostatic height error for the stated standing posture.

giancoli-ch10-q74.answer: (a) Height = (ρHg/ρfluid)(52 mm) = 0.707 m. (b) A pressure of 680 mm-H₂O requires 0.680 m of this water-density fluid. (c) To just balance a 75-mm-Hg vein gauge pressure, h = 1.02 m; actual inflow requires slightly more height to overcome flow resistance.

giancoli-ch10-q76.answer: Estimated bottom-to-top pressure difference = ρairgh ≈ 1.29(9.80)(380) = 4.8 × 10³ Pa, about 0.047 of sea-level atmospheric pressure. This treats air density as constant over 380 m.

giancoli-ch10-q78.answer: Estimated uncompensated force ≈ ΔPA = ρairgΔh A = 1.29(9.80)(1250)(0.20 × 10⁻⁴) = 0.32 N. The direction depends on ascent or descent; this constant-density estimate is approximate.

giancoli-ch10-q80.answer: Required ideal pressure head h = v²/(2g) = 9.2²/(2 × 9.80) = 4.3 m of water above the faucet. This assumes a large supply reservoir with negligible surface speed and ignores viscosity.

giancoli-ch10-q82.answer: Handle force ranges from about 103 N to 152 N. Use F = PgaugeA with A = π(0.025)²/4 and gauge pressures 210 and 310 kPa, neglecting seal friction.

giancoli-ch10-q84.answer: The model continent projects about 5.3 km above the mantle. Its submerged fraction is ρcontinent/ρmantle = 2800/3300, so exposed thickness = 35[1 − 2800/3300] km.

giancoli-ch10-q86.answer: At most 72 whole 68-kg people in this ideal model. Total log volume = 12π(0.45)²(6.5)/4 = 12.4 m³, and the useful mass capacity at complete submersion is (1000 − 600)V ≈ 4962 kg, or 72.97 people. Seventy-three would exceed the threshold. This neglects lashings and requires a positive freeboard margin for practical use.

giancoli-ch10-q88.answer: Average hydraulic output power ≈ PΔV × beat rate = [105(133.322)](70 × 10⁻⁶)(70/60) = 1.14 W. This is pressure–volume mechanical power, not the heart's total metabolic consumption.

giancoli-ch10-q90.answer: Water height = (ρalcohol/ρwater)(16.0 cm) = 0.79(16.0) = 12.6 cm above the shared bottom, assuming the liquids remain separated as posed.

giancoli-ch10-q92.answer: Required upper-surface flow speed ≈ √[vlower² + 2mg/(ρairA)] = √[95² + 2(1.7 × 10⁶)(9.80)/(1.29 × 1200)] = 175 m/s. This is the question's simplified uniform-pressure Bernoulli lift model.

giancoli-ch10-q94.answer: Estimated outward force ≈ ΔPA = ½ρairv²A = ½(1.29)(180/3.6)²(2.0 × 3.0) = 9.7 × 10³ N. This follows the stated fixed indoor pressure and ideal outdoor Bernoulli-pressure assumptions; actual storm loads depend on building geometry and flow.

giancoli-ch10-q96.answer: Block three-quarters of the opening, leaving one-quarter open, if volume flow stays approximately constant. At the same horizontal launch height, time of fall is unchanged and range is proportional to exit speed, so a fourfold range needs fourfold speed. Continuity then gives Anew/Aold = 1/4. Without approximately fixed flow, supply pressure and losses affect the result.

giancoli-ch10-q98.answer: (a) Initial outlet speed ≈ √[2g(0.44 m)] = 2.94 m/s: the outlet is 0.40 m below the sink bottom and initially 0.44 m below the water surface. (b) Emptying time is about 13 s. A constant initial-flow estimate gives 12.5 s; integrating the falling head from 0.44 to 0.40 m gives 12.8 s. Use sink area 0.38 m² and tube area π(0.023)²/4, neglecting viscosity.
